# Introduction {#intro}

![](/images/gy_chili.png){ width=15% style="float:right; padding:10px" }

This tutorial introduces **power analysis** in R — a method for determining whether a study design is capable of detecting a real effect, and if so, with what probability. Power analysis is used both *before* data collection (to determine the sample size needed) and *after* data collection (to evaluate whether a null result may reflect insufficient statistical power rather than a genuine absence of effect).

The tutorial covers power analysis for common statistical tests using the `pwr` package [@pwr], for mixed-effects models using the `simr` package [@simr], and for a broader range of designs using the `WebPower` package. It draws on examples from psycholinguistics (reaction time experiments), sociolinguistics (survey studies), and the mixed-effects modelling context introduced in the original LADAL regression tutorial. A worked end-to-end example in the style of a pre-registration — justifying the significance threshold, estimating the expected effect size, determining the required sample size, and reporting the results — concludes the tutorial.

A list of highly recommended papers discussing effect sizes and power analyses in linguistic research can be found [here](http://crr.ugent.be/archives/2014). The present tutorial draws on @green2016simr, @brysbaert2018power, @arnold2011simulation, and @johnson2015power as key references.

::: {.callout-note}
## Prerequisite Tutorials

Before working through this tutorial, we suggest you familiarise yourself with:

- [Getting Started with R](/tutorials/intror/intror.html) — R objects, basic syntax, RStudio orientation
- [Basic Inferential Statistics in R](/tutorials/basicstatz/basicstatz.html) — t-tests, chi-square, ANOVA
- [Mixed-Effects Regression in R](/tutorials/regression/regression.html) — lmer and glmer modelling
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial you will be able to:

1. Explain what statistical power is and what determines it
2. Distinguish between a priori, sensitivity, and post-hoc power analysis
3. Interpret and convert between common effect size measures (Cohen's *d*, *f*, *w*, *f*², odds ratio)
4. Perform power analyses for t-tests, chi-square tests, ANOVA, and GLMs using the `pwr` package
5. Perform power analyses for a wider range of designs using the `WebPower` package
6. Conduct simulation-based power analysis for mixed-effects models using `simr`
7. Generate and interpret power curves to determine the minimum adequate sample size
8. Write a pre-registration-style power analysis justification
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Citation

Schweinberger, Martin. 2026. *Power Analysis in R*. Brisbane: The Language Technology and Data Analysis Laboratory (LADAL). url: https://ladal.edu.au/tutorials/pwr/pwr.html (Version 2026.05.01).
:::

# What Is Statistical Power? {#concepts}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** The definition of statistical power and Type I/II errors; why power matters for the replicability of linguistic research; the three factors that jointly determine power (effect size, sample size, variability); and key findings from large-scale power analyses in psychology and linguistics
:::

## The Four Outcomes of a Hypothesis Test {-}

Every statistical test can have one of four outcomes, depending on whether the null hypothesis ($H_0$) is true or false and whether the test rejects it or not:

|  | $H_0$ is **true** | $H_0$ is **false** |
|---|---|---|
| **Reject $H_0$** | Type I error (false positive, rate = $\alpha$) | Correct rejection (**power** = $1 - \beta$) |
| **Fail to reject $H_0$** | Correct retention (rate = $1 - \alpha$) | Type II error (false negative, rate = $\beta$) |

**Statistical power** ($1 - \beta$) is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis — in other words, the probability that a study *finds* a real effect when one truly exists. By convention, a power of at least **0.80** (80%) is considered the minimum acceptable standard for most research contexts [@cohen1988statistical; @field2007making]: this means a 20% chance of missing a real effect.

The **significance level** $\alpha$ is the tolerated Type I error rate — typically set at 0.05 (5%). $\alpha$ and power trade off: lowering $\alpha$ (e.g. to 0.01) makes it harder to reject $H_0$ and therefore reduces power unless the sample size is increased.

## What Determines Power? {-}

Three factors jointly determine the power of a study:

**Effect size** is the magnitude of the phenomenon being studied — the distance between population means, the strength of a correlation, or the size of a group difference. Larger effects are easier to detect. Effect size is the one factor researchers typically have the least control over: it is a property of the phenomenon, not the design.

**Sample size** (or the number of observations) is the most direct lever researchers have. More observations reduce sampling variability and make it easier to distinguish a real effect from noise. In designs with both participants and items (as in most psycholinguistics and corpus-based experiments), *both* the number of participants and the number of items contribute to power.

**Variability** in the data (captured by the standard deviation or residual variance) competes with the signal. Lower variability makes effects easier to detect. Repeated-measures and mixed-effects designs reduce effective variability by accounting for between-participant and between-item differences.

The relationship between these factors is formalized differently for each test type, but the intuition is always the same:

$$\text{Power} = f\!\left(\frac{\text{Effect size} \times \sqrt{N}}{\text{Variability}}\right)$$

## Power in Linguistic Research {-}

@brysbaert2018power conducted a large-scale simulation study of the power of experiments in experimental psychology and psycholinguistics and reached the following key conclusions:

- In experiments with repeated measures per participant per condition, replicable results can sometimes be achieved with as few as 20 participants — *if* each participant contributes enough observations.
- A **ballpark figure of 1,600 observations per condition** (e.g., 40 participants × 40 stimuli) is recommended for reaction time experiments starting a new line of research where the expected effect size is unknown.
- Standardised effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's *d*) computed over participants depend on the number of stimuli presented. This has direct implications for replication studies and meta-analyses.

These findings highlight that linguistic research, like psychology, has historically been underpowered — a major contributor to the replication crisis.

## A Priori, Sensitivity, and Post-Hoc Power Analysis {-}

Power analysis can be used in three distinct modes:

**A priori power analysis** (the most common and most valuable) determines the **sample size** needed to achieve a target power (e.g., 0.80) given an assumed effect size and significance level. This is the pre-study planning tool.

**Sensitivity analysis** determines the **minimum detectable effect size** given a fixed sample size, significance level, and target power. This is useful when the sample size is constrained (e.g., a rare clinical population) and the researcher needs to know what effect magnitudes the study can realistically detect.

**Post-hoc power analysis** — sometimes called *observed power* — estimates power based on the observed effect size from the data just collected. This approach is widely considered misleading [@hoenig2001abuse; @perugini2018practical] because the observed effect size is itself an unreliable estimate, particularly in small samples. It should be treated with extreme caution and is not a valid defence of a non-significant result.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Post-Hoc Power Is Not a Valid Diagnostic

A non-significant result does *not* become meaningful simply because a post-hoc power calculation returns low power — this is circular reasoning. The appropriate response to a non-significant result is either (a) to increase the sample size before re-testing, or (b) to report a confidence interval or equivalence test to bound the effect size.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercises: Statistical Power Concepts
:::

**Q1. A study has 80% power to detect a medium effect. If the true effect in the population is small (not medium), what happens to the actual power of the study?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "concepts_q1"
check_question(
  "Power decreases — a smaller effect is harder to detect with the same sample size",
  options = c(
    "Power increases — smaller effects are more common so they are easier to detect",
    "Power stays at 80% — it was calculated for this study design",
    "Power decreases — a smaller effect is harder to detect with the same sample size",
    "Power becomes undefined — you can only calculate power for the effect size you assumed"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "concepts_q1",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! Power is always calculated relative to a specific effect size. If the true effect is smaller than the one assumed in the power calculation, the study has less power than intended. This is why researchers should use conservative (smaller) effect size estimates when planning studies in new research areas.",
  wrong = "Not quite. Power is a function of effect size, sample size, and variability. If the true effect is smaller than assumed, the signal-to-noise ratio decreases and the study is less likely to detect it — power falls below the target level."
)
```

---

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "concepts_q2"
check_question(
  "Determining the smallest effect size a study can detect given a fixed N, alpha, and target power",
  options = c(
    "Estimating power after data collection using the observed effect size",
    "Determining the smallest effect size a study can detect given a fixed N, alpha, and target power",
    "Calculating the sample size needed for 80% power given an assumed effect size",
    "Testing whether the assumptions of the statistical model are met"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "concepts_q2",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! A sensitivity analysis asks: given that I have (or can recruit) N participants, what is the minimum effect size I can reliably detect? This is especially useful when the sample size is constrained by practical factors such as participant availability, cost, or access to a rare population.",
  wrong = "Not quite. A sensitivity analysis works backwards from a fixed sample size to determine the minimum detectable effect size. It is distinct from a priori power analysis (which finds N) and from post-hoc power analysis (which uses observed data)."
)
```

# Effect Size Measures {#effectsizes}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** The most commonly used effect size measures in linguistic research — Cohen's *d*, Cohen's *f*, Cohen's *w*, *f*², and the odds ratio; their conventional small/medium/large thresholds; how to convert between them; and which measure is appropriate for which test
:::

## Why Effect Sizes Matter {-}

Effect sizes are standardised, scale-free measures of the magnitude of a relationship or difference. They serve two purposes: (1) they allow meaningful comparison across studies with different measurement scales, and (2) they provide the input to power calculations. Reporting effect sizes alongside *p*-values is now a formal requirement in most linguistics and psychology journals [@gries2005kilgariff].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Language Is Never Random

@kilgarriff2005language made the pointed observation that *language is never, ever, ever, random*. In sufficiently large corpora, even trivially small differences between conditions will yield statistically significant results — because with enough data, the null hypothesis of randomness is always false. This is why **effect size** rather than *p*-value is the appropriate metric for deciding whether a result is *meaningful*, not merely *detectable*. Always report both.
:::

## Cohen's *d* {-}

Cohen's *d* is used for comparing two means (t-tests). It expresses the difference between means in units of standard deviations:

$$d = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\sigma_{\text{pooled}}}$$

Conventional benchmarks [@cohen1988statistical]: small $d \geq 0.2$, medium $d \geq 0.5$, large $d \geq 0.8$.

In **psycholinguistic reaction time (RT) experiments**, for example, a condition difference of 30 ms with a within-participant SD of 120 ms corresponds to $d = 30/120 = 0.25$ — a small effect.

## Cohen's *f* {-}

Cohen's *f* is used for one-way ANOVA and related designs. It is the ratio of the standard deviation of group means to the within-group standard deviation:

$$f = \frac{\sigma_{\text{means}}}{\sigma_{\text{within}}}$$

Conventional benchmarks: small $f \geq 0.1$, medium $f \geq 0.25$, large $f \geq 0.4$.

## Cohen's *w* {-}

Cohen's *w* is used for chi-square tests of independence and goodness of fit:

$$w = \sqrt{\sum_{i} \frac{(P_{1i} - P_{0i})^2}{P_{0i}}}$$

Conventional benchmarks: small $w \geq 0.1$, medium $w \geq 0.3$, large $w \geq 0.5$.

## *f*² (Cohen's *f*-squared) {-}

*f*² is used for linear regression and GLMs. It is derived from $R^2$:

$$f^2 = \frac{R^2}{1 - R^2}$$

Conventional benchmarks: small $f^2 \geq 0.02$, medium $f^2 \geq 0.15$, large $f^2 \geq 0.35$.

## Odds Ratio {-}

The **odds ratio (OR)** is the natural effect size for logistic regression and chi-square tests on binary outcomes. It expresses how much more likely outcome A is relative to outcome B across two groups. The correspondence with Cohen's *d* [@chen2010big; @cohen1988statistical] is approximate:

| Denomination | Cohen's *d* | Odds Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Small | 0.2 | 1.68 |
| Medium | 0.5 | 3.47 |
| Large | 0.8 | 6.71 |

## Converting Between Effect Sizes in R {-}

The `effectsize` package provides convenient conversion functions:

```{r efconv, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(effectsize)

# Cohen's d → odds ratio
d_to_oddsratio(0.2)   # small
d_to_oddsratio(0.5)   # medium
d_to_oddsratio(0.8)   # large

# odds ratio → Cohen's d
oddsratio_to_d(1.68)

# r → d
r_to_d(0.1)
r_to_d(0.3)
```

## Extracting Effect Sizes from Tests {-}

The `effectsize` package can extract effect sizes directly from test objects:

```{r efextract, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# generate two RT-style vectors: control vs. primed condition
set.seed(2026)
rt_control <- rnorm(40, mean = 620, sd = 120)
rt_primed  <- rnorm(40, mean = 580, sd = 120)

tt <- t.test(rt_control, rt_primed)
effectsize::cohens_d(rt_control, rt_primed)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercises: Effect Size Measures
:::

**Q3. A sociolinguistic survey finds that 60% of Group A and 50% of Group B use a particular variant. Is this likely to correspond to a small, medium, or large effect (Cohen's *w*)?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "es_q1"
check_question(
  "Small — a 10 percentage point difference typically corresponds to a small w",
  options = c(
    "Large — a 10 percentage point difference is always practically significant",
    "Medium — proportional differences of this size correspond to w ≈ 0.3",
    "Small — a 10 percentage point difference typically corresponds to a small w",
    "It cannot be determined without knowing the total sample size"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "es_q1",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! A 10-percentage-point difference in proportions (60% vs. 50%) typically yields a Cohen's w in the small range (around 0.1). The effect size w is a standardised measure that does not depend on sample size — but sample size determines whether we can detect it reliably. Small effects require large samples.",
  wrong = "Not quite. Cohen's w measures the standardised distance between observed and expected proportions. A 10-percentage-point difference between two groups (60% vs. 50%) is a small effect, typically w ≈ 0.10. Large samples are needed to detect small effects with adequate power."
)
```

---

**Q4. A researcher uses `effectsize::cohens_d()` and obtains *d* = 0.45. What does this mean, and which conventional size category does it fall into?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "es_q2"
check_question(
  "The means differ by 0.45 pooled standard deviations — this is a small-to-medium effect",
  options = c(
    "45% of the variance in the outcome is explained by the group difference",
    "The means differ by 0.45 pooled standard deviations — this is a small-to-medium effect",
    "The probability of a correct classification is 45% above chance",
    "The odds of the outcome are 0.45 times higher in one group than the other"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "es_q2",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! Cohen's d expresses the difference between two means in standard deviation units. d = 0.45 means the means differ by 0.45 pooled SDs — larger than small (0.2) but below medium (0.5), so it falls between those conventional categories. It is not a proportion of variance explained (that would be eta-squared or R-squared).",
  wrong = "Not quite. Cohen's d is a standardised mean difference: d = (mean1 - mean2) / pooled_SD. A value of 0.45 means the means are 0.45 standard deviations apart. The conventional thresholds are small ≥ 0.2, medium ≥ 0.5, large ≥ 0.8 — so d = 0.45 falls between small and medium."
)
```

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "pwr", "WebPower", "lme4",
                   "sjPlot", "simr", "effectsize", "DT",

# What Determines Whether You Find an Effect? {#determinants}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** A visual and intuitive exploration of how effect size, sample size, and variability each independently influence whether a statistical test can detect a real effect
:::

To build intuition before running formal power calculations, we simulate distributions and compare them under varying conditions. The helper function below generates two samples and plots their distributions alongside t-test results:

```{r distfun, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
distplot <- function(mean1, mean2, sd1, n,
                     pop = "two different populations",
                     d = 0, effect = "no",
                     ylim = 0.06, seed = 123) {
  require(tidyverse)
  require(DescTools)
  set.seed(seed)
  dat <- data.frame(
    time  = c(rnorm(n, mean1, sd1), rnorm(n, mean2, sd1)),
    group = rep(c("Group A", "Group B"), each = n)
  ) |>
    dplyr::group_by(group) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      mean = mean(time),
      cil  = DescTools::MeanCI(time, conf.level = 0.95)[2],
      ciu  = DescTools::MeanCI(time, conf.level = 0.95)[3]
    ) |>
    dplyr::ungroup()

  ttest  <- t.test(time ~ group, data = dat)
  label  <- paste0("t = ", round(ttest$statistic, 2),
                   ", df = ", round(ttest$parameter, 1),
                   ", p = ", round(ttest$p.value, 4))

  ggplot(dat, aes(x = time, colour = group, linetype = group)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_point(aes(x = mean, y = 0.05)) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = cil, xmax = ciu, y = 0.05, height = 0.005)) +
    annotate("text", x = 120, y = 0.05, label = label, size = 3.5) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(60, 140), ylim = c(0, ylim)) +
    labs(
      title = paste0(effect, " effect | d = ", d,
                     " | N = ", n, " per group | SD = ", sd1),
      x = "Reaction time (ms)", y = "Density", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}
```

## Effect Size {-}

We hold sample size (N = 30 per group) and variability (SD = 10) constant and vary the effect:

```{r efsize_weak, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Two groups sampled from the same population — no true effect."}
distplot(mean1 = 100, mean2 = 100, sd1 = 10, n = 30,
         pop = "the same population", d = 0, effect = "none", seed = 123)
```

```{r efsize_small, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Small effect (d = 0.2): means differ by 2 ms, SD = 10."}
distplot(mean1 = 99, mean2 = 101, sd1 = 10, n = 30,
         d = .2, effect = "small", seed = 111)
```

```{r efsize_medium, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Medium effect (d = 0.5): means differ by 5 ms, SD = 10."}
distplot(mean1 = 97.5, mean2 = 102.5, sd1 = 10, n = 30,
         d = 0.5, effect = "medium", seed = 222)
```

```{r efsize_large, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Large effect (d = 0.8): means differ by 8 ms, SD = 10."}
distplot(mean1 = 96, mean2 = 104, sd1 = 10, n = 30,
         d = 0.8, effect = "large", seed = 444, ylim = 0.08)
```

**Key insight:** If variability and sample size remain constant, larger effects are easier to detect.

## Sample Size {-}

We hold the effect (d = 0.5) and variability (SD = 10) constant and vary N:

```{r n30, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="N = 30 per group: medium effect often missed."}
distplot(mean1 = 97.5, mean2 = 102.5, sd1 = 10, n = 30,
         d = 0.5, effect = "medium", seed = 555)
```

```{r n100, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="N = 100 per group: medium effect reliably detected."}
distplot(mean1 = 97.5, mean2 = 102.5, sd1 = 10, n = 100,
         d = 0.5, effect = "medium", seed = 888)
```

**Key insight:** If variability and effect size remain constant, larger samples increase power.

## Variability {-}

We hold the effect (d = 0.5) and N constant and vary the standard deviation:

```{r sd10_2, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="High variability (SD = 10): medium effect harder to detect."}
distplot(mean1 = 97.5, mean2 = 102.5, sd1 = 10, n = 30,
         d = 0.5, effect = "medium", seed = 888)
```

```{r sd5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Low variability (SD = 5): medium effect much easier to detect.", fig.height=4}
distplot(mean1 = 97.5, mean2 = 102.5, sd1 = 5, n = 30,
         d = 0.5, effect = "medium", ylim = 0.125, seed = 999)
```

**Key insight:** If sample size and effect size remain constant, lower variability increases power.

# Basic Power Analysis with `pwr` {#basicpwr}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** How to use the `pwr` package to perform a priori power analysis and sensitivity analysis for the most common statistical tests used in linguistics: one-way ANOVA, general linear models, paired and independent t-tests, and chi-square tests
:::

The `pwr` package [@pwr] implements the analytical power formulas from @cohen1988statistical. Each function takes three of the four parameters (effect size, sample size, significance level, power) and solves for the fourth. The functions covered here are:

| Test | Function | Effect size |
|---|---|---|
| One-way ANOVA | `pwr.anova.test()` | Cohen's *f* |
| General linear model | `pwr.f2.test()` | Cohen's *f*² |
| Paired t-test | `pwr.t.test()` | Cohen's *d* |
| Two-sample t-test (unequal N) | `pwr.t2n.test()` | Cohen's *d* |
| Chi-square test | `pwr.chisq.test()` | Cohen's *w* |

## One-Way ANOVA {-}

**Scenario:** A sociolinguistic survey compares attitudes toward a language variety across 5 regional groups. We expect a moderate effect (*f* = 0.25), use $\alpha$ = 0.05, and target 80% power.

```{r bp01, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(pwr)

# A priori: how many participants per group?
pwr.anova.test(
  k         = 5,    # number of groups
  f         = 0.25, # moderate effect
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power     = 0.80
)
```

The minimum sample size is **40 participants per group** (200 total). If we could only recruit 30 per group, the power would be:

```{r bp02, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Sensitivity check: power with N = 30 per group
pwr.anova.test(k = 5, f = 0.25, sig.level = 0.05, n = 30)
```

With 30 per group, power drops to about **67%** — insufficient by convention.

**Sensitivity analysis:** What is the smallest *f* detectable with 30 per group at 80% power?

```{r bp03, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.anova.test(k = 5, n = 30, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.80)
```

With 30 per group, only effects of *f* ≥ 0.30 (between moderate and large) can be reliably detected.

## General Linear Model (GLM/Regression) {-}

**Scenario:** A regression model with 2 predictors is fit to data from 60 participants ($df_{\text{numerator}}$ = 2, $df_{\text{denominator}}$ = 57). We want to know the power for detecting a small effect (*f*² = 0.02).

```{r ex1, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.f2.test(
  u         = 2,    # df numerator
  v         = 57,   # df denominator
  f2        = 0.02, # small effect
  sig.level = 0.05
)
```

Power is only about **17%** — dramatically underpowered for a small effect.

## Paired t-Test {-}

**Scenario (psycholinguistics):** A priming study measures RT before and after a priming manipulation in 30 participants. We expect a small RT advantage of about 25 ms (SD ≈ 125 ms, giving *d* ≈ 0.2).

```{r ex2, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.t.test(
  d           = 0.2,
  n           = 30,
  sig.level   = 0.05,
  type        = "paired",
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
```

Power is only about **17%** for a small effect with 30 participants. How many do we need?

```{r ex2b, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.t.test(
  d           = 0.2,
  power       = 0.80,
  sig.level   = 0.05,
  type        = "paired",
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
```

We need **199 participants** to reliably detect a small priming effect of *d* = 0.2.

## Independent Samples t-Test {-}

**Scenario (sociolinguistics):** A survey compares the frequency of a pragmatic marker between two speaker groups: 35 younger speakers and 25 older speakers. The hypothesis is directional (the marker is more frequent among younger speakers), corresponding to a one-tailed test.

```{r ex3, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.t2n.test(
  d           = 0.2,
  n1          = 35,
  n2          = 25,
  sig.level   = 0.05,
  alternative = "greater"
)
```

Power is around **18%** — far too low to trust a null result.

## Chi-Square Test {-}

**Scenario (corpus linguistics):** A 2×2 contingency table tests whether word order (SOV vs. SVO) differs between two registers. We use a small effect (*w* = 0.2) with $\alpha$ = 0.05.

```{r ex4, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.chisq.test(
  w         = 0.2,
  N         = 100,  # total observations
  df        = 1,
  sig.level = 0.05
)
```

Power is about **29%** with 100 observations. What total N would yield 80% power?

```{r ex4b, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
pwr.chisq.test(
  w         = 0.2,
  power     = 0.80,
  df        = 1,
  sig.level = 0.05
)
```

We need **197 total observations** to reliably detect a small corpus frequency difference.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercises: Basic Power Analysis
:::

**Q5. A researcher plans a paired t-test with 50 participants to detect a medium effect (*d* = 0.5, two-tailed, $\alpha$ = 0.05). What is the expected power?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "basicpwr_q1"
check_question(
  "Around 97% — a medium effect with 50 participants in a paired design is highly detectable",
  options = c(
    "Around 50% — medium effects always require very large samples",
    "Around 70% — just below the 80% threshold",
    "Around 97% — a medium effect with 50 participants in a paired design is highly detectable",
    "Around 80% — by definition, medium effects need exactly 80% power"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "basicpwr_q1",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, n = 50, sig.level = 0.05, type = 'paired', alternative = 'two.sided') returns power ≈ 0.97. With a medium effect and 50 participants in a repeated-measures design, power is excellent. This is consistent with the intuition that repeated-measures designs are more powerful than between-subjects designs for the same N.",
  wrong = "Not quite. Try running: pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, n = 50, sig.level = 0.05, type = 'paired', alternative = 'two.sided'). A paired design with 50 participants and a medium effect gives excellent power — well above the 80% threshold."
)
```

---

**Q6. A corpus study finds a statistically significant chi-square result (*p* = 0.03) with a total of 5,000 observations. A colleague argues this means the finding is linguistically important. What is the most important additional check?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "basicpwr_q2"
check_question(
  "Compute the effect size (Cohen's w) — with 5,000 observations, even a negligibly small effect can be significant",
  options = c(
    "Increase the sample size further to confirm the result",
    "Report a confidence interval for the p-value",
    "Compute the effect size (Cohen's w) — with 5,000 observations, even a negligibly small effect can be significant",
    "Re-run the test with a Bonferroni correction"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "basicpwr_q2",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! This is exactly the scenario Kilgarriff (2005) warned about. With 5,000 observations, a chi-square test will detect effects of w ≈ 0.04 at 80% power — an effect so small it is unlikely to be linguistically meaningful. Always compute and report the effect size alongside the p-value.",
  wrong = "Not quite. With large corpora, even trivially small differences become statistically significant. The appropriate response is to compute Cohen's w (or a similar effect size) to assess whether the significant result is also *meaningfully* large. As Kilgarriff (2005) noted, language is never random — large enough samples will always reject the null."
)
```

# Power Analysis with `WebPower` {#webpower}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** How to use the `WebPower` package for power analysis of designs not covered by `pwr`, including one-sample and two-sample proportion tests, mediation analysis, and multilevel/repeated-measures designs commonly used in psycholinguistics and sociolinguistics
:::

The `WebPower` package [@webpower] provides power analysis for a wider range of designs and is particularly useful for repeated-measures ANOVA and proportion tests that appear frequently in survey-based sociolinguistic research.

## Two-Proportion Z-Test {-}

**Scenario:** A sociolinguistic survey tests whether the proportion of speakers using a particular feature differs between two communities (60% vs. 50%). We plan to recruit 150 speakers per community.

::: {.callout-note}
`wp.prop()` uses **Cohen's *h*** as its effect size — not raw proportions. Cohen's *h* is computed from two proportions using `pwr::ES.h(p1, p2)`. Always convert first.
:::

```{r wp01, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(WebPower)

# wp.prop() uses Cohen's h as its effect size, not raw proportions.
# Convert p1 = 0.60 and p2 = 0.50 to h using ES.h() from the pwr package:
h_60_50 <- pwr::ES.h(0.60, 0.50)
h_60_50

wp.prop(
  h           = h_60_50,
  n1          = 150,
  n2          = 150,
  alpha       = 0.05,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  type        = "2p"
)
```

With 150 per community, we have modest power to detect this 10-percentage-point difference. Let's find the required N:

```{r wp02, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
wp.prop(
  h           = h_60_50,
  n1          = NULL,   # to be solved
  alpha       = 0.05,
  power       = 0.80,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  type        = "2p"
)
```

## Repeated-Measures ANOVA {-}

**Scenario (psycholinguistics):** A within-subjects reading time experiment has 3 conditions. We assume a medium effect (*f* = 0.25), $\alpha$ = 0.05, and estimate the correlation between repeated measures as 0.5.

```{r wp03, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
wp.rmanova(
  n         = NULL,   # to be solved
  ng        = 3,      # number of groups/conditions
  nm        = 3,      # number of measurements per participant
  f         = 0.25,
  nscor     = 0.5,    # sphericity correction (Greenhouse-Geisser)
  alpha     = 0.05,
  power     = 0.80
)
```

## Mediation Analysis {-}

**Scenario:** A study tests whether social network integration mediates the relationship between dialect contact and phonological accommodation. We expect path coefficients *a* = 0.3 and *b* = 0.3.

```{r wp04, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
wp.mediation(
  n     = NULL,
  a     = 0.3,
  b     = 0.3,
  varx  = 1,
  vary  = 1,
  alpha = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercises: WebPower
:::

**Q7. Two dialect surveys recorded feature use as follows: Region A: 45%, Region B: 35%. Using `wp.prop()`, approximately how many speakers per region are needed to detect this difference with 80% power ($\alpha$ = 0.05, two-tailed)?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "webpower_q1"
check_question(
  "Around 370 per region",
  options = c(
    "Around 50 per region — small differences are easy to detect",
    "Around 150 per region",
    "Around 370 per region",
    "Around 1,000 per region — proportion differences always require huge samples"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "webpower_q1",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! First convert the proportions to Cohen's h: ES.h(0.45, 0.35) ≈ 0.10. Then wp.prop(h = 0.10, n1 = NULL, power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, alternative = 'two.sided', type = '2p') returns approximately n = 370 per group. A 10-percentage-point difference corresponds to a small h, requiring a substantial sample.",
  wrong = "Not quite. wp.prop() requires Cohen's h, not raw proportions. First run ES.h(0.45, 0.35) to convert, then pass the result as h. A 10 percentage-point difference is a small effect (h ≈ 0.10), which requires around 370 speakers per region to detect with 80% power."
)
```

---

**Q8. In a repeated-measures design, why is power typically higher than in an equivalent between-subjects design with the same number of participants?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "webpower_q2"
check_question(
  "Because between-participant variability is removed from the error term, increasing the signal-to-noise ratio",
  options = c(
    "Because repeated-measures tests use a less conservative significance threshold",
    "Because participants in repeated-measures designs always show larger effects",
    "Because between-participant variability is removed from the error term, increasing the signal-to-noise ratio",
    "Because WebPower uses a different formula than pwr for repeated measures"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "webpower_q2",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! In a repeated-measures design, each participant serves as their own control. Individual differences in baseline performance (e.g. some people are generally faster readers) are factored out of the error term. This reduces residual variance and makes the effect-to-noise ratio larger — increasing power for the same N.",
  wrong = "Not quite. The key advantage of repeated-measures designs is that they partial out stable between-participant differences from the residual error. Because participants serve as their own controls, the error variance is smaller, and the same effect size is easier to detect."
)
```

# Advanced Power Analysis with `simr` {#simrpwr}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** How to conduct simulation-based power analysis for linear mixed-effects models (`lmer`) and generalised linear mixed-effects models (`glmer`) using the `simr` package; how to extend a pilot model to larger samples and plot power curves; and how to test power for fixed effects and interactions
:::

Simulation-based power analysis is essential for mixed-effects models because no closed-form analytical power formula exists for designs with crossed random effects. `simr` [@simr] works by: (1) defining a model with specified fixed and random effects, (2) simulating many datasets from that model, and (3) fitting the model to each simulated dataset and recording how often the target effect is significant.

## Using Piloted Data and `lmer` {-}

We load piloted data from a psycholinguistic experiment that recorded which characters appeared in scenes of a play (serving here as a proxy for participant-by-item designs). The data contains `Group`, `SentenceType`, and `WordOrder` as predictors with participants (`ID`) and items (`Sentence`) as crossed random effects.

```{r reg01, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
regdat <- base::readRDS("tutorials/power/data/regdat.rda", "rb")
head(regdat, 8)
str(regdat)
```

```{r reg02, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# check design balance
table(regdat$Group, regdat$WordOrder)
table(regdat$Group, regdat$SentenceType)
```

### Setting Model Parameters {-}

We specify effect sizes for fixed effects and variances for random effects. The fixed effects are set to 0.52 — we verify below that this corresponds to a small-to-medium effect (OR ≈ 1.68, Cohen's *d* ≈ 0.2):

```{r reg03, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fixed <- c(.52, .52, .52, .52, .52)   # intercept + 4 slopes
rand  <- list(0.5, 0.1)               # random intercept variances for Sentence and ID
res   <- 2                             # residual SD
```

```{r reg03b, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# verify: exp(0.52) is the odds ratio
exp(0.52)
# corresponds to a small effect:
oddsratio_to_d(exp(0.52))
```

### Fitting the Simulated Model {-}

```{r reg04, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m1 <- makeLmer(
  y ~ (1 | Sentence) + (1 | ID) + Group * SentenceType + WordOrder,
  fixef   = fixed,
  VarCorr = rand,
  sigma   = res,
  data    = regdat
)
sjPlot::tab_model(m1)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The summary confirms that the parameter values are correctly specified, but none of the effects are significant yet — this is expected for a pilot dataset that is underpowered by design.
:::

### Power for a Main Effect {-}

We test power for `WordOrder` using `fcompare`, which compares the full model to a model without that predictor:

```{r reg06, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
sim_wo <- simr::powerSim(
  m1,
  nsim = 20,
  test = fcompare(y ~ Group * SentenceType)
)
sim_wo
```

::: {.callout-warning}
We use only `nsim = 20` here for speed. In practice, use at least 500–1,000 simulations for reliable estimates. With 20 simulations, the confidence intervals on power estimates are very wide.
:::

### Power for an Interaction {-}

```{r reg10, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
sim_gst <- simr::powerSim(
  m1,
  nsim = 20,
  test = fcompare(y ~ WordOrder + Group + SentenceType)
)
sim_gst
```

## Extending the Design: Adding Items {-}

Since power is insufficient, we extend the model to explore what sample size is needed. We first increase the number of sentences (items):

```{r ext01, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m1_as <- simr::extend(m1, along = "Sentence", n = 120)
```

```{r ext03, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
sim_m1_as_gst <- powerSim(
  m1_as, nsim = 20,
  test = fcompare(y ~ WordOrder + Group + SentenceType)
)
sim_m1_as_gst
```

### Power Curve over Items {-}

```{r ext04, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Power curve for the Group:SentenceType interaction as a function of the number of sentences (items)."}
set.seed(2026)
pcurve_items <- simr::powerCurve(
  m1_as,
  test   = fcompare(y ~ WordOrder + Group + SentenceType),
  along  = "Sentence",
  nsim   = 20,
  breaks = seq(20, 120, 20)
)
plot(pcurve_items)
```

## Extending the Design: Adding Participants {-}

```{r ext13, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m1_ap <- simr::extend(m1, along = "ID", n = 120)
```

```{r ext15, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
sim_m1_ap_gst <- powerSim(
  m1_ap, nsim = 20,
  test = fcompare(y ~ WordOrder + Group + SentenceType)
)
sim_m1_ap_gst
```

### Power Curve over Participants {-}

```{r ext17, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Power curve for the Group:SentenceType interaction as a function of the number of participants."}
set.seed(2026)
pcurve_pp <- simr::powerCurve(
  m1_ap,
  test   = fcompare(y ~ Group + SentenceType + WordOrder),
  along  = "ID",
  nsim   = 20,
  breaks = seq(20, 120, 20)
)
plot(pcurve_pp)
```

## Simulation-Based Power for `glmer` {-}

**Scenario:** A binary-outcome eye-tracking experiment (fixation: yes/no) with 10 participants, 10 items, and 2 conditions (Control vs. Test).

```{r glmer01, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
simdat <- data.frame(
  Subject   = rep(paste0("Sub",  1:10), each = 20),
  Item      = as.character(rep(1:10, 20)),
  Condition = rep(c(rep("Control", 10), rep("Test", 10)), 10)
) |> dplyr::mutate_if(is.character, factor)

head(simdat, 12)
```

```{r glmer02, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fixed_glm <- c(.52, .52)
rand_glm  <- list(0.5, 0.1)

m2 <- simr::makeGlmer(
  y ~ (1 | Subject) + (1 | Item) + Condition,
  family  = "binomial",
  fixef   = fixed_glm,
  VarCorr = rand_glm,
  data    = simdat
)
sjPlot::tab_model(m2)
```

```{r glmer04, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
rsim_m2_c <- powerSim(m2, fixed("ConditionTest", "z"), nsim = 20)
rsim_m2_c
```

### Extending Items and Plotting the Curve {-}

```{r glmer06, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m2_ai <- simr::extend(m2, along = "Item", n = 40)
```

```{r glmer08, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Power curve for ConditionTest as items increase from 10 to 40."}
set.seed(2026)
pcurve_m2_ai <- powerCurve(
  m2_ai,
  fixed("ConditionTest", "z"),
  along  = "Item",
  nsim   = 20,
  breaks = seq(10, 40, 5)
)
plot(pcurve_m2_ai)
```

### Extending Participants and Plotting the Curve {-}

```{r glmer10, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m2_ap <- simr::extend(m2, along = "Subject", n = 40)
```

```{r glmer12, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Power curve for ConditionTest as participants increase from 10 to 40."}
set.seed(2026)
pcurve_m2_ap <- powerCurve(
  m2_ap,
  fixed("ConditionTest", "z"),
  along  = "Subject",
  nsim   = 20,
  breaks = seq(10, 40, 5)
)
plot(pcurve_m2_ap)
```

### Increasing Observations per Cell {-}

In repeated-measures designs each participant–item combination may occur more than once. Increasing repetitions can be more practical than recruiting new participants:

```{r glmer14, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Power curve as the number of observations per Subject:Item cell increases from 2 to 10."}
m2_reps <- simr::extend(m2, within = "Subject+Item", n = 10)

set.seed(2026)
pcurve_reps <- powerCurve(
  m2_reps,
  fixed("ConditionTest", "z"),
  within = "Subject+Item",
  nsim   = 20,
  breaks = seq(2, 10, 2)
)
plot(pcurve_reps)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercises: Simulation-Based Power Analysis
:::

**Q9. You run `powerSim()` with `nsim = 20` and get power = 75% (15/20 significant). Should you trust this estimate?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "simr_q1"
check_question(
  "No — with only 20 simulations the confidence interval is very wide; use at least 500 simulations for reliable estimates",
  options = c(
    "Yes — 20 simulations is sufficient for a preliminary estimate and 75% is close to 80%",
    "No — with only 20 simulations the confidence interval is very wide; use at least 500 simulations for reliable estimates",
    "Yes — simr is calibrated so that 20 simulations gives the same result as 1,000",
    "No — powerSim always underestimates power when nsim is low, so the true power is higher"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "simr_q1",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! With nsim = 20, the 95% confidence interval for a power estimate of 75% spans roughly 51% to 91% — far too wide to be actionable. The simr documentation and Green & MacLeod (2016) recommend at least 500–1,000 simulations for a reliable power estimate. Use nsim = 20 only for fast exploratory runs.",
  wrong = "Not quite. Power estimates from simulations are proportions (significant / total), so their precision depends on the number of simulations. With 20 simulations, the binomial 95% CI for 15/20 = 75% runs from about 51% to 91%. This is far too wide to conclude that power is near 80%. Use at least 500 simulations."
)
```

---

**Q10. In a crossed participant-by-item design, you can increase power by adding more participants, more items, or more observations per cell. Which is most practical when participant recruitment is expensive?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "simr_q2"
check_question(
  "Adding more items or more observations per cell, since these increase power without requiring additional participants",
  options = c(
    "Adding more participants — this is always the most effective strategy",
    "Adding more items or more observations per cell, since these increase power without requiring additional participants",
    "None of the above — power can only be increased by lowering alpha",
    "It does not matter — all three contribute equally to power"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "simr_q2",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! In a crossed participant-by-item design, power is determined by both participant N and item N. When participants are expensive or hard to recruit (as in studies of rare populations, clinical groups, or heritage speakers), adding more items or more repeated exposures per item-participant pair can substantially increase power without requiring additional recruitment.",
  wrong = "Not quite. Power in mixed-effects models depends on the number of observations at all levels of the design. When participant recruitment is expensive, increasing the number of items or the number of observations per participant-item cell is an effective alternative. The `simr::extend(within = ...)` argument allows you to model this."
)
```

---

# Post-Hoc Power Analysis {#posthoc}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** When post-hoc power analysis is appropriate and when it is misleading; how to fix effect sizes to represent theoretically motivated small effects rather than observed effects; and how to extend observed data to determine what sample size would be needed to detect a real effect
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Post-Hoc Power Is Circular

Post-hoc power analysis using the *observed* effect size from the same data is methodologically circular and gives misleading results [@hoenig2001abuse; @perugini2018practical]. If the test was non-significant, the observed effect size is likely an underestimate; plugging this into a power calculation will return low power — but this tells you nothing you did not already know from the non-significant p-value. The preferred approach is to (a) set the effect to a theoretically motivated value (e.g. the smallest effect of interest), and (b) use simulations to determine whether the *existing* data would be sufficient to detect *that* effect.
:::

We generate simulated eye-tracking data with a binary outcome (fixation on the AOI: yes/no) and fit a glmer:

```{r glmer20, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
simdat2 <- simdat |>
  dplyr::arrange(Condition) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    AOI = factor(c(
      sample(c("yes", "no"), 100, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.5, .5)),
      sample(c("yes", "no"), 100, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.7, .3))
    ))
  )
head(simdat2, 12)
```

```{r pwr77, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
m3 <- glmer(
  AOI ~ (1 | Subject) + (1 | Item) + Condition,
  family = "binomial",
  data   = simdat2
)
sjPlot::tab_model(m3)
```

### Fixing Effects to a Theoretically Motivated Value {-}

Rather than using the observed effect, we set the effect of `ConditionTest` to exactly represent a small effect (OR = 1.68, *d* ≈ 0.2):

```{r pwr81, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
fixef(m3)["ConditionTest"] <- 0.519   # log(1.68) ≈ 0.519

# confirm
exp(fixef(m3))
```

Now we check whether the data can detect this small effect:

```{r pwr82, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
m3_pwr_se <- powerSim(
  m3,
  fixed("ConditionTest", "z"),
  nsim = 20
)
m3_pwr_se
```

Power is insufficient. We extend the data to find the required sample size:

```{r pwr83, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m3_ai <- extend(m3, along = "Item", n = 30)

m3_ai_pwr <- powerSim(
  m3_ai,
  fixed("ConditionTest", "z"),
  nsim = 20
)
m3_ai_pwr
```

```{r glmer36, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Power curve showing how power increases as items are added to the eye-tracking study."}
set.seed(2026)
pcurve_m3 <- powerCurve(
  m3_ai,
  fixed("ConditionTest", "z"),
  along  = "Item",
  breaks = seq(5, 30, 5),
  nsim   = 20
)
plot(pcurve_m3)
```

With about 25–30 items (and 10 participants), power approaches the 80% threshold for detecting a small effect.

---

# Worked Example: Pre-Registration Style {#prereg}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** How to write a complete, pre-registration-style power analysis justification — including the choice of significance threshold, the source and rationale for the expected effect size, the power calculation, and the resulting sample size — for a realistic psycholinguistic experiment
:::

The following is a self-contained worked example modelled on the format recommended for pre-registration on platforms such as OSF (Open Science Framework) and AsPredicted.

---

## Research Question {-}

We investigate whether **syntactic priming** affects reading times in a self-paced reading study comparing passive and active sentence completions. Participants read a prime sentence (passive or active) followed by a target sentence, and reading times at the critical region are recorded.

## Step 1: Specify the Significance Threshold {-}

We use the conventional **two-tailed $\alpha$ = 0.05**. Because this is a single primary hypothesis with no multiple comparisons, no correction is applied. We will report the exact p-value and a 95% confidence interval regardless of significance.

## Step 2: Estimate the Expected Effect Size {-}

We base our effect size estimate on @pickering1998implicit, who found syntactic priming effects in self-paced reading of approximately **25–40 ms** on the critical region. Across multiple studies, the within-participant SD of reading times at the critical region is approximately 120–150 ms. Taking a conservative estimate of SD = 150 ms and a priming advantage of 30 ms:

$$d = \frac{30}{150} = 0.20$$

This corresponds to a **small effect** (*d* = 0.20). We use this conservative estimate deliberately: if the effect is larger in our sample, we will be overpowered, which is a better problem than being underpowered.

```{r prereg01, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# verify the effect size
effectsize::d_to_oddsratio(0.20)   # confirm it is "small"
```

## Step 3: Calculate the Required Sample Size {-}

We target **80% power** ($\beta$ = 0.20) for a paired t-test (within-participants priming comparison, two-tailed):

```{r prereg02, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
pwr.t.test(
  d           = 0.20,
  power       = 0.80,
  sig.level   = 0.05,
  type        = "paired",
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
```

The required sample size is **199 participants**. To account for expected dropout (approximately 10%), we will recruit **220 participants**.

## Step 4: Sensitivity Check {-}

With 220 participants in the final analysis, the minimum detectable effect is:

```{r prereg03, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
pwr.t.test(
  n           = 199,
  power       = 0.80,
  sig.level   = 0.05,
  type        = "paired",
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
```

The study is powered to detect effects of *d* ≥ 0.20 — consistent with our target effect. Any effect smaller than *d* = 0.20 would not be detectable and would also be of questionable linguistic significance given the noise in reading time data.

## Step 5: Reporting Template {-}

The following template can be used directly in a manuscript methods section:

> *Power analysis.* We conducted an a priori power analysis using the `pwr` package (Champely, 2020) in R. Based on previous syntactic priming studies (Pickering & Branigan, 1998), we estimated a small-to-medium effect of *d* = 0.20. Using a two-tailed paired t-test design with $\alpha$ = .05 and target power of .80, the required sample size is *N* = 199 participants. We recruited 220 participants to account for an anticipated dropout rate of approximately 10%.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercises: Pre-Registration Power Analysis
:::

**Q11. Your effect size estimate comes from a single small pilot study (*N* = 15) that found *d* = 0.65. Why might using *d* = 0.65 directly in your power calculation be problematic?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "prereg_q1"
check_question(
  "Small pilot studies overestimate effect sizes due to sampling variability; using d = 0.65 will likely result in an underpowered main study",
  options = c(
    "Because d = 0.65 is too large to be biologically plausible in linguistics",
    "Small pilot studies overestimate effect sizes due to sampling variability; using d = 0.65 will likely result in an underpowered main study",
    "Because pilot data should never be used to estimate effect sizes — only published meta-analyses should be used",
    "It is not problematic — a pilot study with 15 participants is sufficient to provide a precise effect size estimate"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "prereg_q1",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! Effect sizes from small samples are noisy estimates of the true population effect. Due to sampling variability, small studies systematically overestimate effect sizes — a phenomenon sometimes called the 'winner's curse'. Using an inflated estimate leads to a sample size that is too small to detect the true (smaller) effect in the main study. Best practice is to use a conservative (smaller) estimate or, if using pilot data, to shrink the estimate toward zero.",
  wrong = "Not quite. The issue is that effect size estimates from small samples (N = 15) are very imprecise and tend to be inflated. If the true effect is smaller than d = 0.65, your main study will be underpowered. Best practice is to use a conservative estimate or prior literature rather than relying on a single small pilot."
)
```

---

**Q12. In your pre-registration you state that you need 199 participants. After data collection, you have 195 due to technical failures. Should you collect more data?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: "prereg_q2"
check_question(
  "It depends — 195 vs 199 is negligible, but if pre-registered as 199, brief justification for the shortfall should be reported",
  options = c(
    "Yes — you must reach exactly 199 or the study is invalid",
    "No — power calculations are approximate anyway, so any N close to 199 is fine with no comment needed",
    "It depends — 195 vs 199 is negligible, but if pre-registered as 199, brief justification for the shortfall should be reported",
    "Yes — you need to restart data collection from the beginning"
  ),
  type = "radio",
  q_id = "prereg_q2",
  random_answer_order = FALSE,
  button_label = "Check answer",
  right = "Correct! Power calculations are approximations, not exact prescriptions. A shortfall of 4 participants (195 vs 199) will not meaningfully change the power of the study. However, transparent reporting matters: if the sample size was pre-registered as 199, note in the paper that 195 participants provided complete data and briefly explain the shortfall. Do not silently change the target N after data collection.",
  wrong = "Not quite. The difference between 195 and 199 participants has a negligible effect on power (the change in power is less than 0.5%). The important principle is transparent reporting: if you pre-registered N = 199, report that you obtained N = 195 and briefly explain why. Do not restart collection, and do not quietly change the pre-registered target."
)
```

# Summary and Further Reading {#summary}

This tutorial has provided a comprehensive introduction to power analysis in R for linguists.

We began with the conceptual foundations: statistical power ($1 - \beta$) is the probability of detecting a real effect, determined jointly by effect size, sample size, and variability. We distinguished between a priori power analysis (to determine sample size), sensitivity analysis (to determine the minimum detectable effect), and post-hoc power analysis (which is generally misleading when based on observed effect sizes).

Effect size measures were covered in depth: Cohen's *d* (for t-tests), *f* (ANOVA), *w* (chi-square), *f*² (regression), and the odds ratio (logistic regression), along with their conventional small/medium/large benchmarks and R functions for conversion and extraction.

Basic power analysis using the `pwr` package was demonstrated for one-way ANOVA, GLMs, paired and independent t-tests, and chi-square tests, using examples from sociolinguistic surveys, psycholinguistic RT experiments, and corpus linguistics.

The `WebPower` package extended coverage to proportion tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, and mediation analysis — designs that frequently appear in survey-based and experimental linguistic research.

Simulation-based power analysis with `simr` was demonstrated for both `lmer` (linear mixed-effects) and `glmer` (generalised linear mixed-effects) models. Power curves showed how power changes as the number of participants, items, or within-cell repetitions is increased — allowing informed decisions about design trade-offs.

A complete pre-registration-style worked example demonstrated how to justify the significance threshold, select a conservative effect size estimate, calculate the required sample size, and report the results in a format suitable for manuscript submission or OSF pre-registration.

**Further reading:** @cohen1988statistical remains the canonical reference for analytical power analysis. @green2016simr is the primary reference for `simr`. @brysbaert2018power is essential reading for experimental psycholinguists. @gries2005kilgariff and @kilgarriff2005language frame the effect size debate for corpus linguistics. For power in generalised additive mixed models, see @baayen2017shadows.
